title: Low-Fat Diet -- Definition/Introduction
content: Low-fat diets are frequently referenced in clinical practice, the scientific literature, and popular media; however, inconsistent definitions have created uncertainty about their appropriate clinical application. While an invited review in the New England Journal of Medicine describes low-fat diets as those providing less than 30% of total daily energy intake, no universally accepted definition exists. Notably, landmark trials such as the Women's Health Initiative Dietary Modification Trial used a more stringent definition, targeting approximately 20% of calories from fat, highlighting the variability underlying commonly cited "low-fat" recommendations. [1]

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Definition/Introduction
content: Very-low-fat diets are more restrictive, typically defined as 15% or less of total energy from fat and sometimes limiting fat intake to 10% or less of daily calories. [2] For example, the Ornish diet provides approximately 10% of total energy from fat, emphasizes a vegetarian eating style with a polyunsaturated-to-saturated fat ratio greater than 1, and allows ad libitum intake of otherwise permitted foods. [1] Even more stringent protocols, such as those used in the Lifestyle Heart Trial, limited fat intake to approximately 7% of total calories. However, such levels may be challenging for patients to sustain over the long term. [2]

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Definition/Introduction
content: Professional society guidelines provide greater clarity. The 2013 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association/The Obesity Society (ACC/AHA/TOS) guideline for obesity management defines lower-fat diets as 30% or less of total calories from fat, a standard used as the comparator in numerous weight-loss trials. [2] Similarly, the AHA Step 1 diet specifies that less than 30% of total calories come from fat and less than 10% from saturated fat, with a prescribed energy restriction. Most plant-based low-fat dietary approaches define low-fat intake as 10% to 15% of total energy from fat, aiming to balance fat restriction with nutritional adequacy at typical caloric intakes.

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Definition/Introduction
content: The AHA's 2023 scientific statement further characterizes very-low-fat dietary patterns as those providing 10% or less of energy from fat, which differ from standard vegan diets by strictly limiting plant-based fat sources such as nuts, seeds, avocados, and liquid oils. [3] The nutrient adequacy of low-fat and very-low-fat diets depends heavily on food selection, and adherence may be challenging because patients must restrict both animal-derived foods and many plant-based fat sources. In some cases, patients require supplementation with fortified foods or nutrients. [1]

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Definition/Introduction
content: Although promoted for weight loss, evidence synthesized in the ACC/AHA/TOS guideline shows that lower-fat (<30%) and higher-fat (>40%) diets produce comparable weight loss at 6 to 12 months when combined with comprehensive lifestyle interventions, underscoring that adherence and caloric balance, rather than macronutrient composition alone, determine weight outcomes. However, these dietary patterns have distinct metabolic effects: lower-fat, higher-carbohydrate diets are associated with greater reductions in low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol and, in some cases, adverse effects on serum triglycerides and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (high-density lipoprotein [HDL] or HDL-C) levels compared with higher-fat, lower-carbohydrate approaches. [2]

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Definition/Introduction
content: Reflecting this evolving evidence base, recent AHA guidance emphasizes improving the quality of dietary fat rather than strictly limiting total fat, recommending replacing saturated and trans fats with monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats. This shift recognizes that strict fat limits are difficult for individuals to sustain and may inadvertently promote increased intake of refined carbohydrates and added sugars. [3] The primary medical indications for prescribing a low-fat diet include severe hypertriglyceridemia (≥750 mg/dL), weight management in patients with obesity or at a healthy weight, and the prevention and management of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. This article reviews these indications in detail and addresses practical considerations for prescribing low-fat diets.

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Issues of Concern
content: Low-fat diets raise several clinical concerns, including nutrient deficiencies, adverse effects on lipid profiles, poor long-term adherence, and unintended dietary substitutions. A common misconception is that fat restriction alone produces greater or more durable weight loss than other diets. Randomized trials and meta-analyses show that low-fat diets do not outperform other calorie-restricted diets for weight loss at 6 to 12 months. Adherence to overall dietary patterns and sustained lifestyle changes are the dominant determinants of success. Overly restrictive fat reduction may also unintentionally increase intake of refined carbohydrates, which can adversely affect triglycerides and glycemic control in some patients. [3] [4]

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Issues of Concern
content: Nutrient deficiency is a key concern, particularly with very-low-fat diets. These diets restrict not only animal-derived foods but also vegetable oils, nuts, seeds, and other plant foods rich in essential fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamins. Without careful food selection, supplementation, or fortification, deficiencies in protein, vitamin B12, essential fatty acids, and other micronutrients may occur. Results from a Korean study found that subjects consuming 15% or fewer of calories from fat had inadequate intake of polyunsaturated fatty acids and significantly lower levels of most nutrients than those consuming higher-fat diets. [5]

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Issues of Concern
content: Adverse effects on lipid profiles and cardiometabolic risk also warrant consideration. Replacing dietary fat with refined carbohydrates can increase triglycerides, lower HDL cholesterol, and contribute to insulin resistance, inflammation, and dyslipidemia. [3] Low-fat, high-carbohydrate diets consistently reduce HDL cholesterol by approximately 3% to 9%, an effect observed across both short- and long-term interventions. [6]  Meta-analyses and controlled trials demonstrate higher HDL levels in patients consuming higher-fat diets, particularly when fat intake includes monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats. In contrast, carbohydrate substitution, especially refined carbohydrates, lowers HDL cholesterol and raises triglyceride levels. [6] [7]

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Issues of Concern
content: Korean population data show a higher prevalence of metabolic syndrome among individuals consuming 15% or less of calories from fat, despite lower overall energy intake, whereas higher fat intake was associated with a reduced risk of most components of metabolic syndrome. [5] The clinical significance of HDL lowering is unclear, as LDL cholesterol often decreases concurrently. However, replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat rather than carbohydrates may better preserve HDL while improving overall cardiometabolic risk profiles.

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Issues of Concern
content: Long-term adherence to restrictive low-fat diets can be challenging. Few patients consistently meet prescribed fat-intake goals. [1] [3] At the population level, reductions in dietary fat intake over recent decades have coincided with rising obesity rates in the United States, underscoring that macronutrient targets alone do not determine outcomes. [8] The reduced satiety of carbohydrate-heavy meals and the widespread availability of processed “low-fat” foods complicate adherence, as these products often contain refined grains, added sugars, and sodium that undermine satiety and metabolic health and hinder caloric reduction. [9]

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Issues of Concern
content: To address these concerns, current clinical guidance generally prioritizes the quality and type of dietary fats consumed over strict limits on total fat intake, except in patients with specific medical indications. The AHA recommends replacing saturated fats with monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats rather than labeling all fats as harmful. [3] Evidence indicates that the benefits of a low-fat diet depend not only on the amount and type of dietary fat but also on carbohydrate quality, with minimally processed, nutrient-dense carbohydrates providing the greatest support for cardiometabolic health. [4] [9]

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Clinical Significance -- Medical Indications for a Low-Fat Diet
content: The primary evidence-based indications for prescribing a low-fat diet include severe hypertriglyceridemia, weight management in patients with obesity or excessive weight, and primary or secondary prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Clinical Significance -- Severe Hypertriglyceridemia
content: In patients with triglyceride levels of 750 mg/dL or higher, particularly those with chylomicronemia, a very-low-fat diet is a critical therapeutic intervention. The National Lipid Association recommends restricting dietary fat to 5% or less of total daily energy for an initial period of 1 to 4 weeks, often in combination with pharmacotherapy, to rapidly reduce triglyceride levels and lower the risk of pancreatitis. Medical nutrition therapy remains the cornerstone of treatment for refractory severe hypertriglyceridemia, regardless of medication use. Once triglyceride levels fall below 750 mg/dL, clinicians may cautiously liberalize dietary fat intake with close biochemical monitoring. [10]

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Clinical Significance -- Weight Management
content: For adults with overweight and obesity, professional society guidelines from the ACC, AHA, and TOS indicate that calorie-restricted low-fat diets (generally fewer than 30% of total calories from fat) produce weight loss comparable to higher-fat dietary patterns when combined with comprehensive lifestyle interventions. [2] Meta-analyses show modest but statistically significant weight loss relative to control diets among patients who follow a low-fat diet for more than 2 months, with an average difference of approximately 3.3 kg. Low-fat diets may also support weight-loss maintenance in some individuals. Importantly, consistent with the 2024 NEJM review, no single dietary pattern demonstrates superiority for weight loss independent of adherence. [1]

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Clinical Significance -- Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease Prevention and Secondary Prevention
content: Dietary interventions play an important role in both the primary prevention of ASCVD by reducing risk among individuals without established disease and in secondary prevention by lowering the risk of recurrent events in patients with known ASCVD. Low-fat diets that specifically reduce saturated fat intake are associated with improvements in cardiometabolic risk factors, including reductions in LDL cholesterol and blood pressure, and have been linked to lower risks of myocardial infarction, diabetes, and all-cause mortality. [1] For patients with metabolic risk factors, the Endocrine Society recommends lifestyle management and a heart-healthy dietary pattern, including limiting saturated fat to less than 7% of total calories. [11] In secondary prevention, the CORDIOPREV trial demonstrated that both low-fat and Mediterranean diets are effective dietary strategies for patients with established coronary heart disease. [12] Similarly, the 2023 ACC/AHA guidelines for chronic coronary disease emphasize healthy dietary patterns that reduce saturated fat intake rather than endorsing a single macronutrient distribution. [13]

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Clinical Significance -- Association Between Dietary Fat Intake and Cancer Risk
content: Epidemiologic studies have long examined associations between dietary fat intake and cancer risk, including breast, prostate, colorectal, and lung cancers. Among these, breast cancer has been the most extensively studied, with observational data suggesting potential links between higher dietary fat intake and risk. [2] [14] Proposed mechanisms include alterations in sex hormone metabolism, oxidative stress and DNA damage, modulation of immune function, and changes in hypothalamic–pituitary signaling that influence endocrine pathways. [15] [16]

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Clinical Significance -- Association Between Dietary Fat Intake and Cancer Risk
content: Accumulating evidence suggests that fat quality may be more relevant to cancer risk than total fat intake. Diets higher in polyunsaturated fatty acids, particularly omega-3 fatty acids, have been associated with potential protective effects. In contrast, some studies' results indicate an increased cancer risk with a higher intake of animal-derived saturated fats. [16] For prostate cancer, dietary fat intake has been hypothesized to influence risk through alterations in circulating sex hormones and related metabolic pathways, which may affect androgen-sensitive tumor growth. [17] Epidemiologic studies' results have correlated higher consumption of animal fat with increased mortality in patients with colorectal cancer, with proposed mechanisms involving altered bile acid secretion and intestinal microbial metabolism. [18] In contrast, populations consuming diets rich in olive oil or marine-derived fats have lower colorectal cancer incidence, further supporting the concept that the type of dietary fat, rather than total fat restriction, may be the more clinically meaningful factor. [19]

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Interventions
content: Effective implementation of low-fat and very-low-fat diets requires a coordinated interprofessional approach that aligns medical indications, dietary implementation, and long-term behavioral support. Physicians and advanced practice clinicians are responsible for identifying appropriate indications for fat restriction (eg, severe hypertriglyceridemia and cardiovascular risk reduction), monitoring clinical response, and integrating dietary therapy with pharmacologic management when indicated. Shared decision-making is essential to ensure that nutritional recommendations reflect patients' goals, comorbidities, and likelihood of adherence.

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Interventions
content: Registered dietitians play a central role in translating macronutrient targets into practical, culturally appropriate meal plans; educating patients on food selection and label interpretation; and ensuring nutrient adequacy, particularly when dietary fat is substantially restricted. For patients prescribed very-low-fat diets, dietitians should assess the need for fortified foods or supplementation to prevent deficiencies in essential fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamins. Pharmacists reinforce dietary counseling for patients receiving lipid- or triglyceride-lowering therapies, identify potential nutrient–drug interactions, and support medication adherence alongside lifestyle modification. Nurses, health coaches, and behavioral health specialists address barriers to adherence, reinforce education over time, and help integrate dietary changes into broader lifestyle interventions that include physical activity, weight management, and cardiometabolic risk reduction.

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Interventions
content: Consistent with contemporary guidance, interprofessional teams should emphasize overall dietary patterns rather than isolated macronutrient targets, except when a specific medical indication necessitates strict fat restriction. Patterns such as the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) style and heart-healthy low-fat approaches prioritize vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, lean protein sources, and low-fat dairy, while limiting refined carbohydrates, added sugars, and processed foods. Regular aerobic physical activity should be encouraged alongside dietary changes to support lipid management, glycemic control, and cardiovascular risk reduction. Clear communication across disciplines is critical to ensure consistent messaging, avoid unintended dietary substitutions (eg, increased intake of refined carbohydrates), and support sustainable, patient-centered care as evidence and guidelines continue to evolve. Sample Low-Fat Meal Plans (approximately 2000 kcal per day)

title: Low-Fat Diet -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Interventions
content: Effective low-fat dietary therapy requires careful attention to patient-specific indications, the type and amount of fat, and the quality of carbohydrates, with interprofessional teams coordinating medical, nutritional, and behavioral strategies. By emphasizing appropriate fat restriction, prioritizing healthy fats, and providing ongoing support, the healthcare team can optimize cardiometabolic outcomes, minimize nutrient deficiencies, and promote sustainable, patient-centered care.
